newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Cocoa's slide offers window to Europe's cash trade.
newsitem.headline: Cocoa's slide offers window to Europe's cash trade.

text.p: This week's gyrations on London's cocoa futures market have been accompanied by pockets of activity by the continental cash trade, with offtake reported from German customers in particular, traders said on Friday.
But the strength of sterling remained a major headache.
It had kept buying to a minimum and meant industry had to pick its moment carefully.
"When prices hit their lows, there was good buying for spot material but it dries up as soon as either the market or the currency goes against you," one trader commented.

The market started the week on the defensive, diving nearly three percent on large-scale speculative liquidation on Monday. It fell to a four-month low of 968 stga tonne on Tuesday, before turning around to trade back above 990 stg on Friday.
Origins were still active in selling into the physical market in Europe, with beans from Ivory Coast, Ghana and Cameroon on offer for new crop positions.
Traders said top quality afloat Ivorian cocoa was changing hands at around 40 stg under the terminal market and Cameroon beans for late summer/early autumn at up to 60 under.
One trader noted a large spot Ivorian deal to a major buyer in the U.S. at $177 over the New York terminal.
The major origins were reported to be well sold, although traders said it was difficult to pinpoint the exact level.
Cocoa arrivals in Amsterdam have tailed off in recent weeks, particularly when compared with last year, when warehouses were struggling to contain a bumper mid-crop from Ivory Coast.
According to data from SGS Europe, inventories in the Dutch port have been falling since early May. From a peak near 640,000 tonnes, the latest survey puts them at 530,000 in early June.
"They're falling by some 75,000 tonnes a month, purely due to normal offtake. But compared to last summer, there's hardly any cocoa arriving at all," one Dutch trade source said.
The physical market for cocoa products remained at a low ebb, with currency factors keeping prices and demand at depressed levels.
Trades cited a cocoa butter ratio over futures of 2.45 for this year and next.
"The problem is that we may have a market below where we were last year but if the buyers are holding marks, they're facing a 30 percent currency swing against them," one said.
